proposedDescription: Tinocallis ulmiparvifoliae is an aphid associated with Chinese elm. Winged individuals have pale blue-green bodies with white wax stripes and spots, and colonies feed on the leaves. Originally associated with Asia, it has also been recorded in Florida as an introduced insect. Its host is a useful clue, but fine anatomical features are needed to distinguish it confidently from other elm-feeding aphids.

proposedDescription: Tuberocephalus sakurae is a tiny aphid associated with cherry trees. Feeding can turn the leaves red or yellow and curl them into sheltered spaces for the insects. Wingless adults on cherry are dark green to black, with brighter young nearby. The species also alternates to underground parts of Artemisia plants. Distorted leaves may be easier to notice than the aphids themselves, but similar damage can have other causes and does not establish the species on its own.

proposedDescription: Uroleucon picridis is a shiny reddish-brown aphid associated with oxtongues in the genus Picris. Colonies may gather on stems just below the flowers. Dark antennae and rear tubes contrast with a paler, yellowish tail-like projection at the end of the body. These details help specialists distinguish it from related aphids. Host identification matters too: some older records from other plants involve similar species, so color alone is not enough for a reliable identification.

proposedDescription: Apple blossom, Cassia javanica, is a tropical tree grown for generous clusters of pink flowers. Its leaves are divided into pairs of leaflets, and its fruit develops into long, cylindrical pods. The tree has a spreading crown and can lose some or all of its leaves seasonally. Several botanical forms differ in their leaves and flower clusters, so a precise identification benefits from photographs of both. Despite its common name, it belongs to the legume family.

proposedDescription: This form of apple blossom belongs to the Cassia javanica group of tropical flowering trees. Botanical references place the older name var. indochinensis under Cassia javanica subsp. agnes. It has paired leaflets and pink flowers, with branching flower clusters at the ends of young leafy shoots. Pink flowers alone cannot separate it from related forms. A comparative study identifies leaflet details, shoot hairs, stipules and flower structures as useful clues, so a confident identification needs a closer look than flower color.

proposedDescription: Arabian schismus is a small annual grass with fine leaves and a short, compact flower head. It grows in dry, open places and disturbed desert ground. In the southwestern United States, its dried growth can help carry fire across spaces between shrubs, especially when seasons of abundant rain produce more vegetation. It closely resembles Schismus barbatus, another introduced desert grass. Small differences in the flower parts are more dependable for separating them than a photograph of their leaves.

proposedDescription: Brachyrhynchus membranaceus is a flat bug associated with fungi and decaying wood. Its flattened body suits the sheltered spaces used by these insects. Originally known from the Old World, it has also been documented in the Caribbean and Central America. It feeds on fungal growth and has sometimes damaged cultivated bracket fungi. Finding this insect around wood does not by itself show that a healthy tree is being attacked; its documented food is fungal tissue.

proposedDescription: Araucaria aphid feeds on young growth of Araucaria trees, including around the bases of needles on fresh shoots. Wingless individuals are broadly oval and bright yellow to orange, measuring only about one to one and a half millimeters long. Their tiny size makes a close look worthwhile. The species has been recorded in several tropical and subtropical regions, but that wide distribution does not clearly identify its original home. The host and color are useful clues rather than a complete diagnosis.

proposedDescription: Araucaria black scale can look like a dark speck attached to a leaf. The female shelters beneath a nearly circular, flattened brown-black cover with darker shed skins near its center. Despite the name, its hosts extend well beyond Araucaria: palms, olives and many other woody plants have been recorded. This broad host range makes examination of the insect especially useful. A dark spot on a familiar plant can suggest an armored scale, but it does not establish this species.

proposedDescription: Arborvitae scale is a tiny armored insect associated with arborvitae, junipers and other conifers. Its cover can be oval or almost round, with a dull greenish-yellow color that becomes paler and browner with age. Infestations may accompany discolored foliage and dying twigs. A Pennsylvania study found a small parasitic wasp attacking this scale, and predatory mites sheltering in the empty scale covers afterward. Those observations reveal a small community around the insect, but do not establish a tested treatment for an infested tree.

proposedDescription: Mining scale can be easy to miss because plant tissue often partly hides its pale, rounded cover. The cover may be white, gray or yellow and is roughly three millimeters across at most. Howardia biclavis feeds on many kinds of woody plants. Researchers studying Mexican avocado orchards found it singly or in very small groups on branches, sometimes alongside other armored scales. Despite its common name, the exact way it becomes covered by plant tissue is not well understood, so it is better described as concealed than as a proven tunneling insect.

proposedDescription: Lepidosaphes pinnaeformis leaves small brown, mussel-shaped covers on the leaves and sometimes stems of its hosts. Orchids are frequent hosts, and dense colonies can leave a patchwork of discolored feeding spots. The insect is not restricted to orchids: a Mexican orchard study also found it on avocado branches. Its covers can look much like those of other Lepidosaphes scales. A close view helps locate the insects, while microscopic features of the female are needed to distinguish similar species reliably.

Heavy infestations sometimes accompany early leaf fall and twig dieback, although damage varies among locations. This is a different insect from Unaspis euonymi, another scale associated with euonymus.

Its narrow, nearly flat tan covers are only about one to two millimeters long, with darker shed skins at one end and a pink or red female underneath. Its sheltered position and resemblance to other scales make microscopic examination important for a reliable identification.

proposedDescription: Aonidiella taxus is an armored scale found on yews, plum-yews and Podocarpus. A pale, partly transparent cover hides the reddish female beneath it, often on the underside of a leaf. Feeding can leave yellow patches around the insects. Its life also involves much smaller visitors: researchers in Japan found several kinds of tiny wasps parasitizing this scale. The cover and host plant offer useful clues, but related scales can look alike and a confident species identification requires microscopic examination.

A British botanical-garden report also found a heavy infestation on an imported Euphorbia kept in a heated glasshouse.

Dense populations can cause yellowing and damaged leaf or fruit tissue. A field study in Brazil found that numbers on rubber trees changed with the season and differed among tree clones, so infestation levels should be assessed in their local setting.

proposedDescription: Ashy pipewort forms a small tuft of very narrow leaves in wet ground. Mature heads are much more useful for recognition, although their tiny flowers still need close examination to distinguish this plant from other pipeworts.

proposedDescription: Ashy geckos are tiny lizards that shelter in leaf litter, beneath bark and among rocks or woody debris, often near buildings. Young animals have bold bands and bright reddish tails; adults become tan to rusty brown with pale speckling. Sphaerodactylus elegans has been introduced to Florida, where other small geckos can complicate identification. Observations from Cuba also describe these geckos hunting flies and ants around a house during daylight. Their changing colors and secretive habits make a clear photograph more useful than a fleeting glimpse.
